lesson.title: Given What We Know: Conditional Probability
lesson.summary: Conditional probability, P(A given B) = P(A and B) divided by P(B), rescales the sample space down to the world where B is true and asks what fraction of that smaller world also satisfies A.
lesson.body:
Conditional probability answers a very specific question: given that we already know event B happened, what is the updated probability that event A also happened? The formula comes directly from rearranging the general multiplication rule covered in the last chapter. That rule stated P(A and B) = P(B) times P(A given B); dividing both sides by P(B) isolates the conditional probability on its own: P(A given B) = P(A and B) divided by P(B). This is usually written P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B), and it works for any two events as long as P(B) is not zero, whether or not A and B are independent.

The formula has a clean intuitive meaning. Conditioning on B means shrinking the entire sample space down to just the outcomes where B is true, treating that smaller world as the new universe of possibilities, and then asking what fraction of that smaller world also satisfies A. Dividing P(A and B) by P(B) is exactly a fraction calculation: it takes the piece of the sample space where both A and B happen and expresses it as a proportion of the piece where B happens at all, rather than as a proportion of the entire original sample space. This is also the precise mathematical definition of independence promised back in the multiplication rule chapter: A and B are independent exactly when P(A given B) equals P(A), meaning learning B happened did not shrink or change the relevant world in any way that affected A's chances.

Two way tables, the same kind of table used to summarize categorical survey data, are a natural home for conditional probability because they lay out every combination of two variables along with row and column totals. Restricting to a single row or column of the table and asking what fraction of it falls into a particular category is conditional probability in action, even for students who have never seen the formula written out.

Suppose a two way table of 100 students records whether each one plays a school sport and whether each one plays a musical instrument. Fifteen students play both a sport and an instrument, 45 play only a sport, 25 play only an instrument, and 15 do neither, so the sport column totals 60 students, the instrument row totals 40 students, and everything sums to 100. Let A be the event a student plays an instrument and B be the event a student plays a sport. From the table, P(A and B) = 15/100 = 0.15, and P(B) = 60/100 = 0.60. The conditional probability formula gives P(A given B) = 0.15 divided by 0.60, which equals 0.25. This matches direct reasoning from the table: among the 60 sport playing students, exactly 15 also play an instrument, and 15/60 also equals 0.25. Compare this to the overall, unconditional probability that a student plays an instrument, P(A) = 40/100 = 0.40. Since 0.25 does not equal 0.40, knowing a student plays a sport actually lowers the estimated chance that they also play an instrument in this group, which means, by the definition established above, that playing a sport and playing an instrument are not independent events in this sample.

Conditional probability is the tool that finally makes precise an idea this entire unit has circled around since the very first chapter on response bias: whether one piece of information changes what you should believe about another. From randomized response splitting answers across two conditional paths, to two dice and two cards, every calculation in this unit has been a conditional probability question in disguise. Formalizing the relationship as P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) gives a single, reliable formula for all of them.
